elements.quote: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we assessed the clinical accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of commercially available Ag-RDTs.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review (and meta-analysis).

elements.quote: we assessed the clinical accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of commercially available Ag-RDTs
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective/review question clearly.
The abstract text retrieved does not state inclusion/exclusion criteria for studies; eligibility criteria appear only in the full text.

elements.quote: We systematically searched multiple databases (PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, medRvix, bioRvix, and FIND) for publications evaluating the accuracy of Ag-RDTs for SARS-CoV-2 up until 30 April 2021.
elements.reason: Information sources are named and the last search date is given.

elements.quote: rated study quality and risk of bias using the QUADAS-2 assessment tool
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the risk of bias assessment method (QUADAS-2).

elements.quote: Descriptive analyses of all studies were performed, and when more than 4 studies were available, a random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity
elements.reason: The abstract describes the methods used to present and synthesize results.

elements.quote: we included 133 analytical and clinical studies resulting in 214 clinical accuracy datasets with 112,323 samples
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies, datasets, and samples.

elements.quote: the pooled AgRDTsensitivity and specificity were 71.2% (95% CI 68.2% to 74.0%) and 98.9% (95% CI 98.6% to 99.1%), respectively
elements.reason: The abstract reports results for the main outcomes (sensitivity and specificity) with supporting numbers.

elements.quote: the pooled AgRDTsensitivity and specificity were 71.2% (95% CI 68.2% to 74.0%) and 98.9% (95% CI 98.6% to 99.1%), respectively
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary estimates with 95% CIs.

elements.quote: Sensitivity increased to 76.3% (95% CI 73.1% to 79.2%) if analysis was restricted to studies that followed the Ag-RDT manufacturers' instructions.
elements.reason: When groups are compared (e.g., IFU-conforming vs non-conforming, Ct value strata, time since symptom onset), the abstract indicates the direction of effect and which group performs better.

elements.quote: Our analysis was limited by the included studies' heterogeneity in design and reporting.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes limitations of the included evidence.

elements.quote: Concerns of bias were raised across all datasets, and financial support from the manufacturer was reported in 24.1% of datasets.
elements.reason: The abstract provides some interpretive statements (e.g., higher sensitivity in IFU-conforming studies, lower Ct values), but an explicit general interpretation of implications (e.g., a conclusions statement) is not fully evident in the retrieved abstract text.
Funding information appears only in a funding footnote within the retrieved chunk, not as part of the abstract content itself.

elements.quote: We registered the review on PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42020225140).
elements.reason: The abstract provides both the register name (PROSPERO) and the registration number.

elements.quote: Initial data from independent evaluations suggest that the performance of SARS-CoV-2 Ag-RDTs may be lower than what is reported by the manufacturers. In addition, Ag-RDT accuracy seems to vary substantially between tests [4-6]. ... Such evaluations differ widely in their quality, methods, and results, making it difficult to assess the true performance of the respective tests [7].
elements.reason: The Introduction describes the current state of knowledge (growing number of Ag-RDTs, independent evaluations showing lower and variable performance) and highlights the uncertainty caused by heterogeneous evaluation quality.

elements.quote: To inform decision makers on the best choice of individual tests, an aggregated, widely available, and frequently updated assessment of the quality, performance, and independence of the data is urgently needed.
elements.reason: The need and importance of the review are explicitly stated, supported also by the Author Summary (text_4): 'To inform decision makers about the best test to choose, an up-to-date summary of their performance is needed.'

elements.quote: While other systematic reviews have been published, they include data only up until November 2020 [8-11], exclude preprints [12], or were industry sponsored [13]. In addition, only 1 assessed the quality of studies in detail, with data up until November 2020 [7,11].
elements.reason: Existing systematic reviews are identified and cited, and the need for the current review (more recent, living, non-industry-sponsored, including preprints) is explained: 'we aim to close this gap in the literature'.
This is a diagnostic accuracy review, not a review of intervention effects; no mechanism-of-action description is required.
Not a review of complex interventions or delivery contexts; a logic model is not applicable to diagnostic test accuracy.

elements.quote: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we assessed the clinical accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of commercially available Ag-RDTs.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the review objective (assessing clinical accuracy of commercially available Ag-RDTs), and the Introduction (text_7) reinforces the aim: 'With our systematic review and meta-analysis, we aim to close this gap in the literature...'. While not framed in a formal framework like PICO, the objective/question is clearly and explicitly stated.

This is a diagnostic accuracy review, not a review of intervention effects; PICO-style planned comparisons do not apply. The review assesses sensitivity and specificity of Ag-RDTs against a reference standard, as stated in text_1.

elements.quote: Weincluded studies evaluating the accuracy of commercially available Ag-RDTs to establish a diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection, against reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) or cell culture as reference standard. We included all study populations irrespective of age, presence of symptoms, or study location. We considered cohort studies, nested cohort studies, case-control or cross-sectional studies, and randomized studies.
elements.reason: Index test, reference standard, populations, settings, and eligible study designs are all explicitly specified.

elements.quote: We included both peer-reviewed publications and preprints.
elements.reason: Publication status (peer-reviewed vs preprints) is specified, but no explicit restrictions on dissemination year or language of publications are stated in the eligibility criteria.

elements.quote: Reports excluded: Ag-RDT not commercially available (n = 34), Guidelines, reviews, modelling (n = 33), Monitoring (n = 24), Use case not diagnosis (n = 20), No estimation of sens. and spec. (n = 14), Did not assess an Ag-RDT (n = 12)...
elements.reason: The PRISMA flow diagram lists 'No estimation of sens. and spec.' as an exclusion reason, which is suggestive but does not explicitly distinguish between outcomes not measured versus outcome results not reported.

elements.quote: Wedifferentiated between clinical accuracy studies (performed on clinical samples) and analytical accuracy studies (performed on spiked samples with a known quantity of virus)... we only considered data from clinical accuracy studies as eligible for the meta-analysis. Separately, we summarized the results of analytical studies and compared them with the results of the meta-analysis for individual tests.
elements.reason: Groups for each synthesis (clinical vs analytical accuracy datasets, with further subgroup/sensitivity analyses) are clearly specified and linked to the review's accuracy comparisons.

elements.quote: Also, publications with a population size smaller than 10 were excluded. Although the size threshold of 10 is arbitrary, such small studies are more likely to give unreliable estimates of sensitivity and specificity.
elements.reason: A rationale is explicitly provided for the notable minimum population size restriction.

elements.quote: We performed the search up until 30 April 2021.
elements.reason: The last search date is reported for all sources searched (databases and FIND website).

elements.quote: We performed a search of the databases PubMed, Web of Science, medRxiv, and bioRxiv using search terms that were developed with an experienced medical librarian
elements.reason: Database names are reported, but no search interface/platform or coverage dates are specified.

elements.quote: Databases (n = 14239) Registers (n = 0)
elements.reason: No study registers or regulatory databases were searched; the PRISMA flow diagram confirms registers = 0.

elements.quote: We also searched the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND) website (https://www.finddx.org/sarscov2-eval-antigen/) for relevant studies manually.
elements.reason: The website name and URL are reported.

elements.quote: We performed a search of the databases PubMed, Web of Science, medRxiv, and bioRxiv
elements.reason: No evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies.

elements.quote: We performed a search of the databases PubMed, Web of Science, medRxiv, and bioRxiv
elements.reason: No individuals were contacted to identify studies according to the reported search strategy.

elements.quote: We performed a search of the databases PubMed, Web of Science, medRxiv, and bioRxiv
elements.reason: No reference list searching is reported in the search strategy.

elements.quote: We performed a search of the databases PubMed, Web of Science, medRxiv, and bioRxiv
elements.reason: No backward or forward citation searching is reported.

elements.quote: We performed a search of the databases PubMed, Web of Science, medRxiv, and bioRxiv
elements.reason: No journals or conference proceedings were hand-searched according to the reported methods.

elements.quote: We performed a search of the databases PubMed, Web of Science, medRxiv, and bioRxiv using search terms that were developed with an experienced medical librarian (M. Grilli) using combinations of subject headings (when applicable) and text-words for the concepts of the search question. The main search terms were 'Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Corona-virus 2,' 'COVID-19,' 'Betacoronavirus,' 'Coronavirus,' and 'Point of Care Testing.' The full list of search terms is available in S2 Text.
elements.reason: Databases and sources searched are named and main search terms reported, with the full strategy deferred to supplementary S2 Text, which is not provided in the retrieved evidence; the complete search strategy as actually run (full strings per database) is therefore not fully reported in the manuscript itself.

elements.quote: We performed the search up until 30 April 2021. No language restrictions were applied.
elements.reason: The date limit and absence of language restrictions are stated, but no justification by reference to eligibility criteria is given, and other potential limits/filters are not discussed.
No published search approaches, filters, or hedge citations, or adaptations of them, are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No natural-language processing or text-analysis tools were reported as used to identify or refine search terms; the search terms were developed with a medical librarian.
No tools for translating search strings between sources are mentioned in the retrieved evidence.
No validation of the search strategy is described in the retrieved evidence.
Although a medical librarian helped develop the search terms, no formal peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is described.

elements.quote: using combinations of subject headings (when applicable) and text-words for the concepts of the search question
elements.reason: The search was based on the concepts of the review question (a PICO-like conceptual structure), so a description of an alternative non-PICO conceptual structure is not required.

elements.quote: Two reviewers (LEB and CE, LEB and SS, or LEB and MB) reviewed the titles and abstracts of all publications identified by the search algorithm independently, followed by a full-text review for those eligible, to select the articles for inclusion in the systematic review.
elements.reason: Two reviewers screened both titles/abstracts and full texts; the number of reviewers is reported for each screening stage.

elements.quote: Two reviewers (LEB and CE, LEB and SS, or LEB and MB) reviewed the titles and abstracts of all publications identified by the search algorithm independently
elements.reason: The text explicitly states the two reviewers worked independently during screening.

elements.quote: Any disputes were solved by discussion or by a third reviewer (CMD).
elements.reason: The disagreement resolution process (discussion or third reviewer) is described.
No retrieved evidence describes contacting study investigators to obtain or confirm eligibility information.
No retrieved evidence describes translation of non-English abstracts or articles for eligibility assessment.
The flow diagram shows 'Records marked as ineligible by automation tools (n = 0)', but no methods text describes the integration of automation tools into the selection process.
No externally derived classifiers are described or identified in the retrieved evidence; the flow diagram reports zero records removed by automation tools.
No internally derived machine learning classifiers are described in the retrieved evidence.
No retrieved evidence describes machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules.
No retrieved evidence describes the use of crowdsourcing platforms in study selection.
No retrieved evidence describes the use of previously screened datasets to eliminate records from screening.

elements.quote: data extraction and the assessment of methodological quality and independence from test manufacturers (see below) was performed by 1 author per paper (SK, CE, SS, or MB) and controlled by a second (LEB, SK, SS, or MB).
elements.reason: Number of reviewers collecting data from each report is explicitly stated (one extractor plus one controller).

elements.quote: At first, 4 authors (SK, CE, SS, and MB) extracted 5 randomly selected papers in parallel to align data extraction methods. Afterwards, data extraction... was performed by 1 author per paper... and controlled by a second.
elements.reason: The independence of the data collection process is described (pilot parallel extraction, then extraction by one author checked by a second, i.e., not fully independent double extraction but the process is reported).

elements.quote: Any differences were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third author (CMD).
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution via discussion or third reviewer is reported.
No process for obtaining or confirming data from study investigators is mentioned.
No automation tools for data collection are reported and there is no indication any were used; the conditional requirement does not apply based on available evidence.
Two studies were in Spanish, but no translation method for data collection is reported.
No software for extracting data from figures is specified.

elements.quote: Studies that assessed multiple Ag-RDTs or presented results based on differing parameters (e.g., various sample types) were considered as individual datasets.
elements.reason: A decision rule for handling multiple reports/datasets is described, but no explicit rule for resolving inconsistencies between multiple reports of the same study is provided.

elements.quote: Wedifferentiated between clinical accuracy studies (performed on clinical samples) and analytical accuracy studies (performed on spiked samples with a known quantity of virus)... while we extracted the data for both kinds of studies, we only considered data from clinical accuracy studies as eligible for the meta-analysis.
elements.reason: Outcome domains (clinical and analytical accuracy, pooled sensitivity and specificity vs RT-PCR per text_2) are identifiable, but full definitions are relegated to S1 Table ('List of data items extracted from studies') which is not detailed in the retrieved text.
No time frame of measurement for the outcome (e.g., timing of index vs reference test, symptom duration as extraction item) is specified in the methods text provided.
The manuscript does not explicitly state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.

elements.quote: Studies that assessed multiple Ag-RDTs or presented results based on differing parameters (e.g., various sample types) were considered as individual datasets.
elements.reason: The handling of multiple results per study is described (datasets split by parameters), which partially implies which results were collected, but no explicit method for selecting among compatible results is stated.
No changes to outcome-domain inclusion or definitions with rationales are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No changes to the processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We assessed heterogeneity by subgroup analyses
elements.reason: Subgroup analyses (Ct value, symptom duration, IFU conformity, sample type, symptoms) indicate which results were considered most important, but the outcomes' prioritisation and its rationale are not explicitly reported.

elements.quote: A full list of the parameters extracted is included in S1 Table, and the data extraction file is available at https://zenodo.org/record/4924035#.YOlzWS223RZ.
elements.reason: The variables sought are deferred to a supplementary table (S1 Table) and a data extraction file rather than being listed and defined in the Methods text itself; the manuscript does not enumerate or define the variables in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Values differ from those provided in the respective paper due to missing or contradictory data. A list including the original data can be found in S2 Table.
elements.reason: Assumptions about missing or unclear information are only indirectly described via a Table 1 footnote (recalculated values where source data were missing/contradictory) and repeated use of 'Unclear' categories in Tables 1 and results; no systematic Methods-section description of assumptions for missing or unclear data is provided.
No tool or instrument used to determine which data items to collect (e.g., a data collection template or existing checklist for data items) is cited anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The quality of the clinical accuracy studies was assessed by applying the QUADAS-2 tool [17].
elements.reason: The tool (QUADAS-2) and its citation are explicitly named.

elements.quote: The tool evaluates 4 domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. For each domain, the risk of bias is analyzed using different signaling questions.
elements.reason: The QUADAS-2 domains and signaling-question approach plus applicability assessment are described.

elements.quote: Fig 2. Methodological quality of the clinical accuracy studies: Risk of bias. Proportion of studies with low, intermediate, high, or unclear risk of bias (percent).
elements.reason: Overall/domain-level risk-of-b judgements (low, intermediate, high, unclear; Fig 2) are reported, but the rules used to derive overall judgements are not explicitly stated.

elements.quote: The QUADAS-2 tool was adjusted to the needs of this review and can be found in S3 Text.
elements.reason: Adaptation of QUADAS-2 is described and the adjusted tool is made accessible in supplementary material.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool; an existing tool (QUADAS-2) was adapted, which is covered under e4.

elements.quote: data extraction and the assessment of methodological quality and independence from test manufacturers (see below) was performed by 1 author per paper (SK, CE, SS, or MB) and controlled by a second (LEB, SK, SS, or MB). Any differences were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third author (CMD).
elements.reason: Number of reviewers, second-reviewer control, and disagreement-resolution procedures are reported; however, the assessment was not fully independent (one primary assessor checked by a second), which is still adequately reported.
No evidence of processes to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators; no indication such contact was attempted, so the requirement does not apply.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment are mentioned; the assessment was performed manually, so this conditional requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: We report point estimates of sensitivity and specificity for SARS-CoV-2 detection compared to the reference standard along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using a bivariate model
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the effect measures for each outcome: pooled sensitivity and specificity with 95% CIs via a bivariate model; univariate random-effects inverse variance meta-analysis for sensitivity-only subgroups; and descriptive ranges when fewer than 4 studies were available.

No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect size magnitude are reported; for diagnostic accuracy measures (sensitivity/specificity) such interpretive thresholds are not a standard requirement and none are described in the evidence.
No re-expression of synthesized results into another effect measure is reported or needed; sensitivity and specificity were used directly throughout.

elements.quote: If 4 or more datasets were available with at least 20 positive RT-PCR samples per dataset for a predefined analysis, a meta-analysis was performed... using a bivariate model... In subgroup analyses where papers presented data only on sensitivity, a univariate random-effects inverse variance meta-analysis was performed
elements.reason: The choice of bivariate versus univariate or descriptive analysis is implicitly justified by data availability (number of datasets, positive samples), but no explicit rationale for choosing the bivariate model as the effect measure is given.

elements.quote: We differentiated between clinical accuracy studies (performed on clinical samples) and analytical accuracy studies (performed on spiked samples with a known quantity of virus). ... while we extracted the data for both kinds of studies, we only considered data from clinical accuracy studies as eligible for the meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes which studies were eligible for each synthesis: only clinical accuracy studies were eligible for meta-analysis while analytical studies were summarized separately (text_14). Additionally, text_17 specifies quantitative eligibility criteria for each synthesis: 'If 4 or more datasets were available with at least 20 positive RT-PCR samples per dataset for a predefined analysis, a meta-analysis was performed' and lists predefined subgroup characteristics (Ct value, IFU conformity, age, sample type, symptoms, symptom duration, viral load, RT-PCR type), with descriptive analysis when fewer than 4 studies were available.

elements.quote: We extracted raw data from the studies and recalculated performance estimates where possible based on the extracted data. ... In an effort to use as much of the heterogeneous data as possible, the cutoffs for the Ct value groups were relaxed by 2-3 points within each range. ... when categorizing by age, the age group < 18 years (children) included samples from persons whose age was reported as < 16 or < 18 years, whereas the age group ≥ 18 years (adults) included samples from persons whose age was reported as ≥ 16 years or ≥ 18.
elements.reason: The methods describe preparing data for synthesis: recalculating performance estimates from raw data, and explicit conversions/groupings of heterogeneous data (Ct value cutoff relaxation and age category harmonization) for subgroup analyses.

elements.quote: A summary of the tests evaluated in clinical accuracy studies, including study identification, sample size, sample type, sample condition, and IFU conformity, can be found in Table 1.
elements.reason: Tables (Table 1, Table 2, S1-S3 Tables) and their content are referenced, but mainly in Results/Supporting Information; the Methods section does not explicitly describe tabulation methods for displaying results.

elements.quote: We prepared forest plots for the sensitivity and specificity of each test and visually evaluated the heterogeneity between studies.
elements.reason: The Methods section describes graphical displays: forest plots for sensitivity/specificity, and the Deeks funnel plot for publication bias; supporting figures (HSROC curves, forest plots, funnel plot) are also listed in the Supporting Information.
No evidence describes the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs.

elements.quote: We also performed the Deeks test for funnel-plot asymmetry as recommended to investigate publication bias for diagnostic test accuracy meta-analyses [18]
elements.reason: Only standard graphs (forest plots, HSROC curves, funnel plots, bar charts) are used; no non-standard graphs are reported, so no rationale for non-standard graphs is required.

elements.quote: using a bivariate model (implemented with the 'reitsma' command from the R package 'mada,' version 0.5.10) ... (using the 'metagen' command from the R package 'meta,' version 4.11-0) ... Analyses were preformed using R 4.0.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria)
elements.reason: Software packages with version numbers (mada 0.5.10, meta 4.11-0, R 4.0.3, Stata 15) are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: When there were fewer than 4 studies for an index test, only a descriptive analysis was performed, and accuracy ranges are reported.
elements.reason: Alternative descriptive synthesis is described with a clear threshold-based rationale.

elements.quote: We report point estimates of sensitivity and specificity for SARS-CoV-2 detection compared to the reference standard along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using a bivariate model
elements.reason: Bivariate model for diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis is named; rationale implied by its suitability for sensitivity/specificity, and a random-effects model is used for univariate subgroups.

elements.quote: a univariate randomeffects inverse variance meta-analysis was performed (using the 'metagen' command from the R package 'meta,' version 4.11-0)
elements.reason: Statistical methods (bivariate model; inverse variance random-effects via metagen) are reported for the meta-analyses.

elements.quote: We prepared forest plots for the sensitivity and specificity of each test and visually evaluated the heterogeneity between studies ... We assessed heterogeneity by subgroup analyses
elements.reason: Heterogeneity was only visually assessed and explored via subgroups; no quantitative measure (e.g., I², tau²) is reported.
The between-study variance estimator for the random-effects meta-analyses is not reported.
The method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect is not described beyond reporting 95% CIs.
No additional random-effects implementation details (e.g., transformation, continuity corrections) are reported.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed; frequentist (bivariate and inverse-variance) methods were used.
No method for handling statistical dependency among multiple datasets/estimates from the same study is described.

elements.quote: Weaimed to do meta-regression to examine the impact of covariates including symptom duration and Ct value range.
elements.reason: Meta-regression was planned but the manuscript does not explicitly state it was judged impossible or give reasons; analytical studies were excluded from meta-analysis with a rationale (text_14), but planned-but-abandoned syntheses are not fully reported.

elements.quote: We assessed heterogeneity by subgroup analyses... We predefined subgroups for meta-analysis based on the following characteristics: Ct value range, sampling and testing procedure in accordance with manufacturer's instructions... age... sample type, presence or absence of symptoms, symptom duration, viral load, and type of RT-PCR used.
elements.reason: Methods to explore heterogeneity (predefined subgroup analyses, meta-regression attempt) are explicitly described in the Statistical Analysis section.

elements.quote: We predefined subgroups for meta-analysis based on the following characteristics: Ct value range... age ( < 18 versus >= 18 years), sample type... symptom duration ( < 7 days versus >= 7 days)...
elements.reason: Factors and their levels are clearly specified (Ct cutoffs, age groups, sample types, symptom duration), but the expected direction of effect modification is not reported.

elements.quote: In subgroup analyses where papers presented data only on sensitivity, a univariate random-effects inverse variance meta-analysis was performed
elements.reason: Subgroup analyses pool dataset-level (study-level) estimates; however, the manuscript does not explicitly state whether analyses used study-level variables or within-study contrasts (e.g., the head-to-head comparisons are discussed in results but not framed as within-study contrast analyses in the methods).

elements.quote: We report point estimates of sensitivity and specificity for SARS-CoV-2 detection compared to the reference standard along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using a bivariate model
elements.reason: No method for formally comparing subgroup effects (e.g., interaction tests or subgroup difference tests) is reported; subgroups are simply pooled and presented side by side.

Given that several authors are affiliated with FIND (a diagnostics foundation funded by manufacturers' stakeholders, per the funding statement in text_2), the disclosure appears incomplete for all authors.

No evidence describes how any competing interests of the review authors were managed in the review process. The only related text concerns assessing independence of included primary studies from test manufacturers, not management of the review authors' own competing interests.

elements.quote: Afull list of the parameters extracted is included in S1 Table, and the data extraction file is available at https://zenodo.org/record/4924035#.YOlzWS223RZ.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that extracted data (data extraction file) and the list of extracted parameters (S1 Table) are available, with extracted data deposited on Zenodo. However, there is no explicit statement covering the public availability of template data collection forms, analytic code, or all other materials used in the review, so availability reporting is only partial.
